# Look it up: plans and computed values are read, not carried {#sec-lookup}

## Rhyme plans {#sec-couplets}

**Task.** Rhyming couplets are the flagship case of latent planning. The model
commits to a rhyme at the end of line 1 and realizes it at the end of line 2
[@lindsey2025biology; @hanna2026latent]. We use the couplet prompts released by
@hanna2026latent and their chat format, with thinking disabled. For Qwen3 1.7B to
14B we use their 100-couplet steering subsets. For Qwen3-32B and Gemma 3 we apply
their selection rule: the first 100 first lines the model rhymes, judged by their
perfect-rhyme criterion. The source is their anchor, the last word of line 1. The
donor is a couplet from a different rhyme group. The target is the position that
predicts the first token of line 2's last word, with the line-2 prefix fixed. We
repeat every run with the plain prompt of @ma2026plan (`A rhyming couplet:` followed
by line 1 and a newline), with no chat template.

**Behaviour.** The all-layer edit of the rhyme word moves line 2 off its rhyme:
after the edit, at most 2% of second lines rhyme with the original, against 83 to
100% before it. It moves line 2 onto the donor's rhyme in 27 to 75% of couplets in
Qwen3 and 62 to 95% in Gemma 3. The emitted line-2 words account for 13 to 25% of the total effect. The rest is persistence: the rhyme position is pushed toward the
donor even when the line-2 words are held fixed.

**Routes.** @fig-couplets decomposes persistence in all 21 runs. Direct retrieval of
the rhyme word is the dominant path: 76 to 95% of persistence in every Qwen3
configuration (1.7B to 32B, chat and plain, instruct and base), and 80 to 95% in
Gemma 3 from 1B to 12B (including the 12B base model). The late lookup through the three positions before the target accounts for 1 to 13%. Early relay, the carrying along the generated line that a text monitor could miss, is at most 1% of persistence in every run, by sufficiency in all 21 and by necessity in the 17 where it was measured. Gemma 3
27B is the exception to retrieval dominance. There, direct retrieval falls to 68%
(chat) and 19% (plain), and two further components appear: a large interaction term
and a copy stored at the line's final token. @sec-storage analyses these
components. They are still lookups from a fixed position of the prompt, not relay
along the generated line.

![Couplet routes across scale, family and prompt format (100 couplets per run).

**The relay that grows with scale is not carrying.** Before running the larger models we committed two criteria for the claim that carrying grows with scale. First,
the relay share must rise with log parameter count across Qwen3 1.7B to 32B. Second,
the rise must come from line-2 positions more than three tokens before the rhyme
word, because the published circuit already retrieves the plan into the last few
positions [@hanna2026latent]. The first criterion holds: the per-couplet relay share
rises by 6.2 percentage points per decade of parameters (95% interval [2.8, 9.6];
medians 4, 8, 8, 11 and 13%). The second fails. Early line-2 relay is \(-0.06\),
\(+0.07\), \(+0.04\), \(-0.01\) and \(+0.16\) at 1.7B, 4B, 8B, 14B and 32B, against
persistence of 12 to 26. By the readings committed in advance, relay does not grow as carrying along the generated text. It grows as the late lookup up to 8B and, from
14B, as a copy at the line boundary (@sec-storage).

**Controls.** Three checks rule out that the split reflects disruption by the edit,
the choice of source position, or the edit type.

- *Same-rhyme donors.* A donor from the same rhyme group leaves the rhyme almost
  unchanged. Persistence is \(+0.1\) to \(+2.0\), against \(+12.1\) to \(+22.6\) with
  different-rhyme donors in Qwen3 1.7B to 8B, and \(+1.6\) against \(+41.2\) in
  Gemma 3 12B. The next-word distribution still changes substantially, so the
  measure tracks rhyme identity, not generic disruption.
- *Anchor specificity.* Donor states at the rhyme word move the rhyme about two to
  three times more than donor states at any other single position of line 1 (the
  first word, a middle word, the punctuation, the end of the turn). Rhyme
  information at those positions is still partly retrieved, at a fifth to a half of
  the anchor's effect. Retrieval is weighted toward the rhyme word rather than
  confined to it.
- *Published feature steering.* We reselect the rhyme features of
  @hanna2026latent with their rule. The mean is 19.1 features per couplet against
  their 19.2, with an exact per-couplet count match on 67 of 100 couplets at 4B. We
  then steer with their protocol instead of editing the state. Direct retrieval accounts for 90%, 88% and 84% of persistence at 4B, 8B and 14B, and relay 8%, 9% and
  14%. The state edit gives the same split (91/10, 90/11 and 82/12), so its strength
  does not drive the result.

The Qwen3.5 hybrids show the same route structure (direct retrieval 84 to 88% of
persistence; @sec-recurrent).

## Computed values {#sec-computed}

A rhyme plan is a property of a visible word. Information that is *computed* is not
present at any single token, and is where relay would seem most useful. We test two
computations with a donor that changes the value (Appendix @sec-app-computed).

**Sums.** The prompt poses a two-digit addition. The model writes an answer-neutral
filler of 0 to 32 tokens and then the answer (104 items per model, Qwen3 1.7B to 32B;
accuracy 95 to 100%). The committed design named the question mark as the position where
the sum would be computed. Donor states there move the answer by \(-0.08\) to
\(+0.07\) log-odds, so the efficacy gate fails at every size. That shows only that the
question mark does not hold the sum. The stronger test edits every position from the
question mark to the answer together: this block moves the answer by at most 6% of the
effect of donor operand digits (\(+17\) to \(+54\); 6% at 32B, at most 3.4% below).
Beyond that, route accounting finds no patch-detectable donor effect downstream, and
the sum is recomputed from the visible operands at the answer.

**Variable chains.** Sums are cheap to recompute. A chain of updates
(`a = 23`, `b = a + 4`, `c = b + 7`, ..., `What is e?`) makes recomputation at the
answer costly and carrying natural. The running value could be passed from
statement to statement, so this task was designed as a second positive-control
candidate for relay. It is not one. Donor states at the starting value's digits move
the answer strongly (at 14B: \(+30.9\), \(+18.5\) and \(+6.4\) for \(K=1,3,5\) updates).
Donor states at any single later position, or at any statement end, move it by less
than 0.4 in absolute value. Donor states at *every* position after the starting value
together, a test that would detect a running value stored redundantly, move it by at
most 2.4% of the source-digit effect (14B, \(K=3\): \(+0.44\) [0.08, 0.82]). In all
other size and length combinations the interval includes zero (@fig-computed). We find
no patch-detectable donor effect at any later position: the answer re-reads the chain.
Accuracy is consistent with recomputation at the answer. It falls steeply with chain
length, from 97 to 100% at \(K=1\) to 1 to 17% at \(K=5\) (Appendix
@fig-computed-extra). We see no sign that the model maintains the running value
downstream even where doing so would make it correct, but this is a correlational
observation, not a test of what the model could do.
